A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same DiVeQ research and contain readable main text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. Existing material can be matched reliably across the expanded appendices and renumbered displays.

before.justification: v1 reports original image compression and generation experiments, including quantitative comparisons, ablations, training analyses, and residual quantization experiments.

after.justification: v2 retains these empirical results and adds original speech coding experiments, additional VQGAN configurations, and replacement and initialization ablations.

M1.justification: The DiVeQ and SF-DiVeQ constructions, detach variants, and importance-based codebook replacement algorithm remain unchanged in Sections 3 and B. v2 explicitly describes SF-DiVeQ's curve-based inference, consistent with its existing construction; this does not establish an algorithm revision. The new initialization experiments vary training settings.

E1.justification: v1 evaluates image compression and generation on five image datasets. v2 retains that coverage and adds speech coding on CSTR VCTK, covering English speech from 109 speakers with different accents using a simplified DAC-based codec (Sections 4 and A.3). This introduces a substantially different modality and task.

E2.justification: The main comparisons retain STE, EMA, RT, ST-GS, and NSVQ. The residual quantization comparisons retain their narrower STE, RT, and NSVQ comparator set. The added speech and robustness experiments introduce no new baseline method.

E3.justification: v2 adds VQGAN training at learning rate 2.5e-4 and batch size 32 alongside the retained 2.5e-5/batch-8 configuration. Speech evaluation introduces speaker-disjoint 80/20 splits, four speech metrics, 300-epoch training, and 10–13-bit codebooks. Sections C.6–C.7 add common initialization without replacement, 100/150/200-epoch comparisons, and codebook learning-rate multipliers of 10–50.

E4.justification: Beyond v1's existing ablations, v2 tests whether DiVeQ's advantages persist without codebook replacement and how SF-DiVeQ depends on initialization, training duration, and codebook learning rate (C.6–C.7, Figures 22–25). It also extends variance sensitivity to VQGAN, adds speech batch-size ablations, and tests VQGAN stability under larger learning rates and batches.

E5.justification: Both versions report three-run averages for image reconstruction and identify selected analyses as individual runs. v2 continues these practices without adding seeds, confidence intervals, error bars, or significance tests. Its speech tables report test-sample averages without specifying a new repeated-run or uncertainty procedure.

E6.justification: Original VQGAN FIDs are retained in the corresponding configuration columns, while v2 adds another configuration, speech results, variance sweeps, and replacement/initialization results. For example, new Table 3 reports 13-bit, batch-64 speech PESQ values of 1.75 for SF-DiVeQ, 1.64 for DiVeQ, and 1.67 for EMA. These are newly reported evaluations with no v1 counterpart.

T1.justification: Section 2 extends the existing two-dimensional NSVQ overshoot argument by asserting that the probability approaches 1 in higher dimensions, without supplying a new derivation. The method equations, gradient expressions, limiting calculations, distortion metric, and appendix RVQ derivations otherwise remain unchanged.

C1.justification: The central contributions remain DiVeQ, SF-DiVeQ, and improved codebook replacement. The abstract, introduction, and conclusion extend the empirical performance claim to DAC-based speech coding. The introduction and Table 1 soften the claim of no hyperparameter tuning to avoiding complicated tuning, and the conclusion drops the blanket tuning claim.

C2.justification: v1 recommends custom SF-DiVeQ initialization; v2 adds substantive explanations of its benefits and limitations, including worse performance with random initialization at larger codebooks and recovery through higher codebook learning rates. Sections C.6–C.7 interpret replacement and convergence effects. Section 4 also limits t-SNE interpretation to intuitive within-method visualization and explains the deliberately simplified speech evaluation.

D1.justification: New Section A.3 documents the speech codec architecture, single codebook, 512-dimensional quantization space, optimizer settings, and VCTK preprocessing, including 16 kHz resampling. v2 adds detailed initialization experiments, explicit SF-DiVeQ inference instructions, a project code URL, and a reproducibility statement describing implementation materials. Existing vision implementation details are largely retained.

R1.justification: v2 adds Vali's 2025 thesis, Vali and Bäckström's 2023 stochastic quantization work, and the VCTK corpus reference. It also foregrounds the already-cited SFVQ inspiration in the introduction. The broader related-work taxonomy and positioning against existing quantization methods remain substantially unchanged.

P1.justification: The main narrative and existing appendix organization remain recognizable. v2 makes targeted grammatical edits, systematically replaces misleading bitrate terminology with codebook bits or size, and revises the misalignment discussion. It inserts speech-related subsections, acknowledgments, a reproducibility statement, and an LLM-use disclosure without extensively rewriting the retained exposition.

P2.justification: v2 substantially expands the visual evidence with new Tables 3 and 8–10 and Figures 22–25. The existing VQGAN tables gain grouped training-configuration columns and failure highlighting. Existing plots receive revised axis labels, variance plots use revised colors, and retained figures and image grids are relocated or renumbered.

improvement.justification: v1 did not separately test dependence on codebook replacement and custom initialization. v2's common-initialization comparison without replacement and initialization sweeps (C.6–C.7) substantially strengthen the evidence while exposing conditions needed for good performance. The additional VQGAN configuration, speech evaluation, and implementation information further improve validation and reproducibility. The main-text summary of random initialization remains broader than Figure 24 supports, and uncertainty reporting remains limited, but the added controls and qualifications provide a substantial net quality improvement.
